subject: chemistry
title: Alcohols: production and properties
key_idea: Alcohols contain the –OH group. They are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary. Hydrogen bonding makes them soluble in water and less volatile than alkanes. Industrially, ethanol is made by hydrating ethene or by fermenting glucose.

blocks.text: Alcohols are classified by the carbon that carries the –OH group. This section covers the three types.

items: Some alcohols contain more than one –OH group, for example ethane-1,2-diol. Classify each –OH group separately.
The type decides how the alcohol is oxidised. See the note on reactions of alcohols.
Count the carbon atoms attached to the C–OH carbon: one, two or three.
Primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols react differently with oxidising agents.

blocks.text: The –OH group gives alcohols properties that alkanes lack. This section explains solubility, volatility, combustion and acidity.

items: The O–H bond is polar. Oxygen is δ– and hydrogen is δ+.
Alcohol molecules form **hydrogen bonds** with each other. Hydrogen bonds are stronger than the London forces between alkane molecules.
More energy is needed to separate alcohol molecules, so alcohols have higher boiling points and lower volatility than alkanes of similar size.
Alcohols form hydrogen bonds with water, so short-chain alcohols dissolve in water.
Solubility falls as the carbon chain gets longer, because the non-polar chain does not form hydrogen bonds.
Alcohols burn in plenty of air to give carbon dioxide and water, for example C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.
Combustion is exothermic, so alcohols are used as fuels.
Hydrogen bonding explains the water solubility and low volatility of alcohols compared with alkanes.
Alcohols burn completely to carbon dioxide and water.

blocks.text: Industrially, alcohols are made from alkenes, or by fermentation. This section covers hydration of an alkene.

blocks.label: Hydration of ethene
where: an acid catalyst, H₃PO₄, is used

items: This is electrophilic addition of steam across the C=C bond.
The reaction is reversible and exothermic. Typical industrial conditions are about 300 °C and 60–70 atm.
Alcohols can also be made by substitution of a halogenoalkane with aqueous alkali, as covered in the halogenoalkane notes.

Carbon-neutral claim: the CO₂ released on burning is equal to the CO₂ absorbed by the plants as they grew. Equations: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, then fermentation, then combustion C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.
Why the claim is not valid: fuel is used for farming, transport, fertiliser and distillation, and these release CO₂.

items: Classify alcohols with more than one –OH group, such as ethane-1,2-diol, by looking at each –OH.
Distinguishing reaction: mild oxidation with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ gives an orange to green colour change with primary and secondary alcohols but not with tertiary alcohols.
Alcohols are very weak acids, weaker than water. They do not react with alkalis.
In an alkoxide ion, RO⁻, the alkyl group pushes electrons towards the oxygen. This makes the negative charge less stable, so ionisation is less likely than for water.
A tertiary alcohol is even less acidic than a primary alcohol, because it has three electron-donating alkyl groups.
